Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate, since Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Operative text retrieved and verified directly from EUR-Lex this run -- Article 3 ("Prohibition of products made with forced labour"): "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The regulation is expressly marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," which is the basis on which Norway is incorporating it. Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29, including forced child labour. The European Commission responded to USTR's final action without retaliation, saying the outcome is in line with the EU-US Joint Statement framework. Source: EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 of 27 November 2024 (primary text); eunews.it, July 24, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; USTR assesses enforcement as inadequate)

Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier but is not yet in force -- it takes effect 30 business days after publication, i.e. approximately mid-August 2026. New detail this run: MINTRAB has said it lacks capacity to conduct extraterritorial investigations and will therefore build that list from international-source information, via a 90-business-day interinstitutional process with the Economy and Foreign Affairs ministries; the list has not been published. The private sector has set out five conditions it wants met on implementation. Classification stays Yes because the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. Source: Prensa Libre, July 27 and 30, 2026; La Hora; Diario de Centro America.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026; NOT yet in force as of July 30, 2026 -- effective 30 business days after publication, ~mid-August 2026; scope limited to imports from a company-specific list which MINTRAB has not yet published)

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express legal prohibition on importing forced-labor-made goods with three enforcement mechanisms (importer declarations, a Ministry of Labour risk list, and binding customs opinions), and requested a 10% "bridge rate" pending completion of its own Reciprocal Trade Agreement. The decree (Art. 4) prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labor, takes effect on publication, and directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system (Art. 7: intercepted goods face re-export or destruction at importer cost); the Labor Ministry's specific prohibited-merchandise list becomes enforceable 30 days after publication (~Aug 16, 2026), with implementing regulations due within the same 30 days. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta (official gazette) No. 37,196, July 17, 2026, via leyes.hn. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026, published in La Gaceta No. 37,196, July 17, 2026; effective on publication, prohibited-goods list enforceable ~Aug 16, 2026)

Summary and Source: Malaysia's 10% tier rests on its US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (signed October 2025), which Minister Johari Abdul Ghani confirmed on July 25, 2026 is signed but not ratified -- the 2-year clock to enact forced-labour import-ban legislation starts only on ratification, and the Human Resources Ministry has been notified of the amendments needed. The earlier "null and void" episode is now explained: per Fulcrum and StratNews, Malaysia's March 2026 declaration followed a February 20, 2026 US Supreme Court ruling striking down IEEPA-based reciprocal tariffs as unconstitutional, and that declaration has since been superseded. That ruling does not disturb this action -- USTR's Federal Register notice rests solely on Sections 301(b) and 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974 and makes no reference to IEEPA (verified directly against the notice text). Ratification nonetheless remains stalled amid domestic backlash, and no forced-labour import-ban bill has been tabled. Source: Malay Mail and New Straits Times, July 25 and 27, 2026; Fulcrum; StratNews; Federal Register doc 2026-15181.

Summary and Source: On July 21, 2026 -- two days before USTR's final determination -- Norway's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries announced a trade ban on products made with forced labour. It covers import, export and sale, and is implemented by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 (marked "Text with EEA relevance") into Norwegian law via the EEA Agreement, in force no later than December 14, 2027; the government committed to that date even if EEA incorporation runs late. As of this run no lovforslag/Proposition has been tabled to the Storting and no Norwegian implementing instrument has been enacted (an earlier hoering on the EU proposal closed with 26 responses), so this remains a government decision rather than an in-force ban. regjeringen.no returns HTTP 403 to automated fetching, so its text has not been read directly; content is confirmed via NRK, NTB and adressa.no. Source: regjeringen.no press release, reported by NRK July 21, 2026 19:41 and wired by NTB July 22, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (formal Norwegian government decision announced July 21, 2026 to ban import/export/sale of forced-labour-produced goods by incorporating EU Regulation 2024/3015 via the EEA Agreement, in force no later than December 14, 2027; no Storting proposition tabled and no Norwegian implementing instrument enacted yet)

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list)
